title: Bell and Cellar
premise: Folklorist Gideon Winterbourne arrives in the isolated village of Hollowmere to record its songs, only to find the villagers refuse to sing any of them twice—and each household keeps a strict nightly count of doors, lights, and names. When an excavation crew unearths a stone door sealed from the inside, the count begins again after a century of silence, and Gideon realizes the 'family' he's been quietly adopted into—the innkeeper Maren, her ward Tansy, and the old sexton Cobb—are marked as the ones who must go below. As villagers vanish one per night in order of their family lines, Gideon uncovers that his own bloodline wrote the original bargain: his ancestor sealed the door from inside, trading himself and his descendants' invisibility for the village's safety. To break the cycle, Gideon must descend willingly before the final count completes, singing the forbidden song twice—once to open the door, once to close it forever—with Maren and Tansy holding the count above. He survives by making the cellar accept a new bargain built on chosen love rather than owed duty, emerging changed but whole as the village finally learns to sing.
about_author: G. M. Reyes is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing funeral hymns and lullabies across remote coastal villages, collecting the songs people were afraid to repeat. Bell and Cellar is their debut novel, drawn from a single field recording no singer would ever perform twice.

chapters.title: The Song You Don't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He arrives in Hollowmere during a rainstorm, welcomed warily by innkeeper Maren, who lets him stay but warns him never to ask anyone to repeat a song. That night he hears the villagers humming something through the walls that stops the moment he listens too closely. Beat: uneasy wonder; the reader feels the village's practiced silence.

chapters.title: Doors, Lights, Names
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He observes the village's rituals: every door counted at dusk, lamps lit in strict order, children reciting family names like prayers. Old sexton Cobb explains it as 'just habit,' but his hands shake doing it. Gideon records his first song—a lullaby Tansy sings once, then refuses forever. Beat: creeping wrongness beneath cozy routine.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A government crew arrives to dig a drainage cut on the moor, led by brisk engineer Halloran, who mocks local superstition. The villagers go quiet in a way Gideon now recognizes as fear, not rudeness. Maren asks him, oddly, whether he has family still living. Beat: intrusion; the protective silence begins to crack.

chapters.title: What the Spade Struck
chapters.summary: Halloran's POV. The crew unearths a granite door set into the hillside, its iron ring fused, its surface scratched—evidence shows the scratches were made from inside. One worker swears he heard counting behind it. That night the village bells ring thirteen times though there are twelve. Beat: dread made physical; the past is exposed.

chapters.title: Sealed From Within
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He examines the door and finds carved tally marks matching the village's nightly counts, ending mid-stroke a century ago. Cobb finally tells him a fragment: long ago, one man went below so the rest could stay above, and the count kept the bargain honest. Beat: revelation of the central rule; Gideon feels personally implicated without knowing why.

chapters.title: Tansy's Second Verse
chapters.summary: Tansy's POV. The orphaned ward dreams of a woman singing underground and wakes with a second verse in her mouth she's never been taught. She sings it once; the lamps gutter in sequence down the lane. Maren burns the transcription and holds Tansy all night. Beat: tenderness and terror entwined; the family bond deepens under threat.

chapters.title: The Count Begins Again
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. At dusk the bells ring of their own accord, and every villager instinctively answers the count aloud—including Gideon, whose name comes out of his mouth before he chooses to speak it. Cobb goes pale: the count hasn't included a Winterbourne in a hundred years. Beat: Gideon is claimed; invisibility ends.

chapters.title: Winterbourne
chapters.summary: Cobb's POV. Cobb reveals the archive he's kept hidden: Gideon's great-grandfather was the one who sealed himself below, and the bargain named his line as keepers—or payment. Gideon's arrival wasn't chance; the letters inviting a folklorist were sent in his ancestors' name. Beat: betrayal and identity crisis; found family vs. blood debt.

chapters.title: First Taken
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The eldest son of the Harrow family doesn't come home; his door stands open, lamp dark, name struck from the count. The village does not search. Maren finds his boots placed neatly at the hillside door, facing inward. Beat: grief and complicity; the horror is administrative, not chaotic.

chapters.title: Halloran's Folly
chapters.summary: Halloran's POV. Refusing to halt work, Halloran orders the door drilled. The drill bits come back warm and wet. His crew quits en masse; alone at night he hears his own name added to a distant count. He seeks out Gideon, humbled and terrified. Beat: skeptic broken; alliance forms between outsider and insider.

chapters.title: The Terms Below
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. In the church crypt, Cobb shows him the original covenant: one from the founder's line descends each hundred years, or the village pays in full. The last keeper went down voluntarily; this time, no one volunteered, so the count collects. Gideon realizes he is both heir and loophole. Beat: stakes clarified; a terrible choice takes shape.

chapters.title: Maren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren tries to offer herself in Gideon's place, claiming him as family so the count might take the head of household instead. The bells ring twice—refusal. She returns home and, instead of despair, begins teaching Tansy the whole forbidden song, note by note. Beat: love against duty crystallizes; preparation replaces panic.

chapters.title: Second Taken
chapters.summary: Tansy's POV. The count takes the schoolmistress, whom Tansy loved. Tansy rages against the village's obedience and nearly runs to the door herself; Gideon stops her, and in the struggle she accidentally teaches him the song's true second verse—the one meant to be sung below, not above. Beat: loss converted into purpose.

chapters.title: What Waits Under Hill
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon and Halloran lower a lantern through the drill hole. What looks back isn't monstrous—it's his great-grandfather, unchanged, still keeping count, still waiting for relief or release. The thing below wears the faces of everyone taken. Beat: horror humanized; the enemy is a system, not a creature.

chapters.title: The Village Decides
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs in rotating paragraphs. A midnight assembly: some want to give Gideon up, some want to flee, Cobb argues for breaking the covenant entirely. Maren's speech—that they've paid a century of fear for safety and gotten neither—turns the room. They choose to help him end it. Beat: justice outside the law; collective courage.

chapters.title: Breaking the Seal
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. On the final night of the count, the village gathers at the door. Gideon sings the first verse; the seal opens inward. His great-grandfather's voice joins his, ragged with a century of loneliness. Below, the taken wait in rows, patient as furniture. Beat: threshold crossed; awe and terror at equal pitch.

chapters.title: The Long Descent
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. He walks the count itself—a corridor of doors, each labeled with a name, each needing to be answered. The house below offers him a place: stay, keep the count, be safe, be needed forever. It shows him visions of belonging he's always lacked. Beat: temptation; the horror offers exactly what he most wants.

chapters.title: Love Against the Ledger
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Gideon and Maren. Above, Maren and Tansy hold the count against the rising pressure to speak his name as taken. Below, Gideon refuses the offered place—not because he fears it, but because he already belongs to people who chose him. He begins the second verse. Beat: climax of theme; choice over inheritance.

chapters.title: Sung Twice
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The second verse completes: the corridor of doors closes one by one, releasing the taken—not back to life, but out of servitude, into rest. His great-grandfather, freed at last, takes Gideon's hand and finishes the count himself, striking his own name last. The door seals—from outside, this time. Beat: catharsis; the debt discharged with mercy.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Bells
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Three days of silence, then Gideon climbs out, gray and diminished but alive. The village buries its dead properly for the first time in a century, reading their names not as a count but as a memorial. Halloran fills the excavation; Cobb burns the covenant. Beat: mourning transformed into ritual; communal healing.

chapters.title: The Song Sung Plainly
chapters.summary: Tansy's POV. At the harvest fire, Tansy sings the lullaby complete, twice through, and nothing happens except that everyone weeps and joins in. Gideon records it—his last act as collector, his first as family. Maren tells him his room upstairs is permanent if he wants it. Beat: warmth earned; the found family formalized.

chapters.title: Bell and Cellar
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, epilogue. A year later, Gideon publishes nothing; some songs belong to the people who survived them. On quiet nights he counts the doors himself—not from fear, but gratitude, each number a name he loves. The bell rings only when rung. The cellar stays shut. Beat: peace with vigilance; the story closes on chosen home.
